About Eric Caskey

Fifteen years in enterprise infrastructure, from a help desk at Prudential Financial to the workflow orchestration and monitoring platforms I own at Amazon. Questions

Common questions

Who is Eric Caskey?
I'm a Senior Software Engineer at Amazon and a platform engineer based in New Jersey. Before Amazon, I worked in remote access and cloud engineering at Prudential Financial. I build production infrastructure that is safe enough to automate, and my independent practice, Caskey Engineering, helps teams assess context, review, and release checks in AI-assisted software delivery.

What does Eric Caskey work on at Amazon?
I own the monitoring platform that standardizes monitors across application stages, and I architected a workflow orchestration platform built safe by default. Its validation guardrails run before every automated change. I also drove the platform's spec-as-code system, which gives AI coding agents curated context instead of raw access.

What has Eric Caskey built outside work?
I built a spec-driven engineering platform that runs my independent practice and a fleet of AI coding agents through a work queue and an attested merge gate, written up as a case study and a lesson series on Caskey Engineering. I also built Ballast, an open-source RAG system with a guardrails gateway, engineered to refuse when it should; SpecSelf, a spec-driven personal operating system whose AI agents read but never write; a C++ Black-Scholes options engine; and a Finance Reviewer where the model narrates numbers it never derives.

How do I contact Eric Caskey?
The contact form at ericcaskey.com/contact is the fastest route. I read everything and reply within a week. You can also find me on LinkedIn at linkedin.com/in/ericrcaskey and on GitHub at github.com/CaskeyCoding.

# About (https://ericcaskey.com/about)

Background · new jersey · since 2011

About

Eric Caskey is a Senior Software Engineer at Amazon with fifteen years in enterprise infrastructure, from the NJ Army National Guard and Prudential Financial to the workflow orchestration and monitoring platforms he owns today. This page is the long version, in his own words.

I came into tech in 2011 through Workforce Opportunity Services (https://medium.com/@wforceorg/success-story-eric-caskey-prudential-financial-d2d2e7258f49), placed at Prudential Financial while I was still serving in the NJ Army National Guard, and taught myself to code on the job. By 2013 I was the Remote Access Analyst: Tier 3 help desk work with a side project generating QR codes for MFA enrollment. That side project ran for eight years and produced over 300,000 activation codes. It also settled which job I wanted: the engineering one, not the support one.

From there I moved up through Remote Access SRE and Senior Remote Access SRE at Prudential, where I built the MFA self-service portal used more than 18,000 times in six languages, automated over 200,000 administrative actions, and kept the VPN running for 60,000 corporate users through the early months of COVID. Most of that work was figuring out how to make safety-critical infrastructure quiet: how to remove failure modes rather than paper over them.

My last year there, from July 2021, was as a Cloud Engineer in Site Reliability Engineering: hands-on AWS and Azure ownership at Fortune 100 scale, building the monitoring flow that alerted leadership channels to global cloud outages in real time and partnering with application teams to unblock deployments between on-prem and the cloud. It was a deliberate pivot, and it is the year that made the next move possible.

In June 2022 I joined Amazon, where I built a monitoring lifecycle platform that onboarded more than 2,750 application stages and brought 3 million monitors under standardized management, and hired and mentored eight new-to-industry engineers in New York. In August 2024 I moved into my current role as a Senior Software Engineer on a platform team, architecting a multi-region workflow orchestration control plane whose guardrails have run 500,000 safety checks, validating every change before it lands. Since then I have mentored engineers on three continents. The lesson carried over from Prudential intact: the platforms worth building are the ones that stay quiet while everything they watch does not.

Outside work I carry the same convictions into an engineering team of one: one engineer, a fleet of AI coding agents, and a spec-driven method where every feature starts as a written spec and nothing merges until it passes the same gate the pipeline runs. Caskey Engineering carries the case studies, a lesson series that teaches the setup one file at a time, the numbers posts that count what it produces and what it costs, and backtests that report what did not work. The builds include Ballast, an open-source RAG system engineered to refuse when it should; SpecSelf, a spec-driven operating system for a life whose agents read but never write; a C++ options engine tuned to 215 million prices a second; and AI finance tools where the model narrates numbers it is never allowed to derive. The selected builds are on the work page (https://ericcaskey.com/work); the full writeups live on Caskey Engineering.

Along the way I ran a New Jersey WordPress shop called Caskey Coding from 2015 to 2018 (ten sites for small businesses and community organizations), and served six years as a Military Police Officer in the 50th Brigade of the NJ Army National Guard, including a 2012 Superstorm Sandy activation where I safeguarded the distribution of 241,000 gallons of FEMA fuel for nearly a month.

Outside of engineering: a dad, a marathoner, and a constant reader on AI and distributed systems.

Values

Guardrails, not booleans.
Safety systems that explain themselves are what keep velocity sustainable past the first incident. Every guardrail I build has to say not just what failed, but why, what would make it pass, and who owns remediation.

Structure before code.
Design before you dive in. Implementation is the fast half; the specs, folder structure, and decision logs that precede it decide whether the system holds up. The structure does not follow the AI; the AI follows the structure.

Scale is the evidence.
A title tells you where someone sits, not what they own. I state mine for context, then let the systems, and the numbers behind them, carry the argument.

Earned lessons only.
I write what I have learned by getting it wrong first, in production. The decisions I would make differently are the ones worth writing about.

Build the systems other engineers depend on. Write honestly about how it goes.

On writing

I publish long-form essays on workflow orchestration, safety-critical platforms, and spec-driven development at Caskey Engineering (https://caskeycoding.com) (caskeycoding.com), including An Engineering Team of One, a lesson series on running a software team of one engineer and a fleet of AI agents. Caskey Engineering is also my independent engineering practice, separate from my role at Amazon. This site covers my career; that one covers the method and the evidence behind it.

For independent work on AI-assisted delivery, explore Caskey Engineering (https://caskeycoding.com/#workflow-assessment).

# Privacy (https://ericcaskey.com/privacy)

Privacy

This site collects as little as it can. Here is exactly what happens with your data.

Analytics

ericcaskey.com uses Google Analytics 4 to count visits and see which pages get read, so Google processes visit data on the site's behalf. It runs in consent mode: for visitors in the European Economic Area, the site tells Google that analytics storage is denied, which is meant to keep analytics cookies off. The site has no setting to change that default. Google's handling of visit data is described in Google's privacy policy (https://policies.google.com/privacy). If a content blocker stops analytics from loading, the pages still work.

Contact form

When you submit the contact form (https://ericcaskey.com/contact), your name, email address, and message are sent to Eric as one email through Amazon Simple Email Service. Nothing is written to a database. Your email address is set as the reply-to so Eric can answer you directly. If the send fails, the error, not your message, may appear in server logs, which AWS keeps for a limited time.

Preferences

Your light or dark theme choice is kept in your browser's local storage so it survives a reload. Links from this site to Eric's other sites, caskeycoding.com and specself.ai, carry the current mode in the address as ?theme=light or ?theme=dark. When you follow one, that value is sent to the destination site so its first page opens in the same mode. That one value is the only addition to those links.

What this site does not do

No accounts, no advertising, and no third-party embeds. Data is not sold or used for advertising. The analytics and email services named above process it as part of running this site.

Questions

Questions about this policy go through the contact page (https://ericcaskey.com/contact).
